evidence.title: Nurse-Led Ambient AI Scribe for Patient Safety Incident Investigation Reports (Project NARRATE): Retrospective Pre-Post Comparative Document-Quality Study
evidence.outcome: WHO-aligned report completeness with workflow including visible missing-information cues
evidence.effect: Completeness 13.61 vs 11.81; cluster-adjusted difference 1.95 (95% CI 0.91-3.00; P<.001); persisted after deformatting (1.70, 95% CI 0.27-3.14). Bundled workflow, voluntary adopters; cue effect not isolated.
evidence.quote: Unadjusted mean WHO total completeness was 11.81 (SD 3.39) for conventional reports and 13.61 (SD 2.54) for NARRATE reports; the unadjusted difference was 1.80 points, and the cluster-adjusted mean difference was 1.95 (95% CI 0.91-3.00; P<.001).

evidence.title: Blinded two-phase evaluation of large language models in complex cardiac surgery: task-specific performance and human-AI collaboration
evidence.outcome: Automation bias from fluent, well-structured LLM outputs suppressing clinician scrutiny
evidence.effect: Overacceptance concentrated in safety-critical dimensions; overacceptance rate 10.16% nearly three times underrecognition 3.68%, net gap +6.48%.

commentary.bottom_line: Twenty-one studies tested interface cues, prompts, or presentation choices meant to promote clinician scrutiny of AI outputs, and results varied by design, with most studies favorable, five null or mixed, and one trial in which explanations failed to reduce and sometimes worsened the effect of misleading AI. Twenty of the studies were offline or simulated, and the one real-deployment study bundled missing-information cues with other workflow changes, so the effect of any specific cue in live care remains uncertain.

perspectives.view: Twenty of 21 tests ran offline or in simulation, many with fewer than 25 clinicians, and the one real deployment used a pre-post design without a comparator. Results were inconsistent across cue types. A behavioral nudge raised reasoning scores by 7.6 points, while a prompt to judge the AI list showed no accuracy gain. These features suggest low certainty.

A box outlining the suspicious region lowered false negatives from incorrect AI from 33.0% to 20.7%, and heatmaps lowered automation bias (aOR 0.56) without eliminating it. With explanations, only 52% of clinicians overrode a wrong recommendation, and in one trial explanations did not blunt misleading AI. The effect of a cue on harm appears to depend on its design.

Disagreeing with the model took a median 84 seconds versus 38 seconds for agreeing, and an interactive coding interface lengthened coding time slightly. A disagreement-guided display cut simulated burden by 4.8% but raised it 12.04% when the false-positive rate reached 0.10. Highlighting error-prone spans reached a positive predictive value of 56.3% and was never tested with clinicians.

The only test tagged as involving a limited English or non-English population enrolled nine clinical coders in China, who showed higher recall and precision with an interactive interface than with black-box predictions. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so the evidence says little about how these cues perform in under-resourced settings.

FDA draft guidance asks manufacturers to describe how configurable elements affect user decisions. In one trial, chain-of-thought output produced more selective adherence than a differential diagnosis list, and in another, suppressing outputs in high-risk zones was estimated to cut automation bias by 41.7%. These findings suggest that presentation settings may warrant documentation and validation.

In the single real deployment, report completeness rose (adjusted difference 1.95 points), but adopters volunteered and the cues were one part of a bundle. Concurrent AI reading saved 33.6 seconds per case with no loss in diagnostic performance compared with second reading. Neither study reports the cost or staffing figures needed to plan adoption across a health system.

In a simulation with a standard editable draft interface, physicians submitted 35% to 45% of erroneous drafts without edits. No supplied study tested whether cues in patient-portal reply drafts reduce the number of errors that reach patients. Patients therefore have little direct evidence that these designs protect the messages they receive.

commentary.research_gap: Health systems need prospective trials in live clinical workflows that test single, well-defined cues against usual interfaces. These trials should measure patient-level errors and harms, clinician time, and whether effects persist as clinicians become familiar with the cues. They should also compare cue designs directly, since some explanation formats appear to help and others appear to hurt.
commentary.underserved_note: One test was tagged as involving a limited English or non-English population, but it was a small vignette simulation with nine clinical coders in China rather than a test with patients. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. The evidence therefore cannot show whether these cues work for clinicians in under-resourced settings or protect the patients those settings serve.
